title: Knowingly Allowed: Six Findings Against a Board That Witnessed and Chose to Ignore

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was taken at the top and the Subcommittee counts it as its own finding: the Board "approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the balance sheet, with the Board’s knowledge. Finding (4): the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." Finding (2) is one sentence long and does the same work: the Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was aimed outward while the Board could see in. The Subcommittee’s first finding records that "The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." The public disclosure that would have shown the liabilities was, on finding (4), not made.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall ran through a vehicle the Board itself authorised. Finding (3): "Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing."
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The check that should have been independent was not. Finding (6): "The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The Subcommittee reached its findings on "over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002" — and it is a congressional report, which determines no liability and adjudicates nothing against any individual director.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A board model in which the audit and compensation committees rely on management’s own presentation of the numbers, and in which directors may hold financial relationships with the company they oversee.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Enron governance regime — audit committee independence requirements, certification of financial statements, and restrictions on auditor conflicts — built directly on findings of this kind.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The off-books structures improved the reported condition; the improved condition supported the compensation the Board approved; the Board that approved it was, on the Subcommittee’s finding, compromised by financial ties to the company whose numbers it was signing off.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Enron was a handful of rogue executives running a scheme nobody upstairs understood — a conjuring trick too clever for its own directors to see.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The Senate Subcommittee found the opposite, twice, in the same word. The Board "knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices", and "knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was". It also found that the Board "witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them", and that it approved — "Despite clear conflicts of interest" — the arrangement under which the chief financial officer ran private funds that "transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense". What should not be drawn from this document is any individual’s liability: it is a congressional subcommittee report, not an adjudication, and it determines none.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Six findings of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, reached on over one million pages of subpoenaed documents and interviews with 13 directors: fiduciary failure; high risk accounting knowingly allowed; inappropriate conflicts of interest in the LJM arrangement approved despite clear conflicts; extensive undisclosed off-the-books activity knowingly allowed, with inadequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities; excessive compensation, including a failure to monitor or halt abuse of a company-financed multi-million dollar personal credit line by the chairman and chief executive; and a board whose independence was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain of its members.

citations.title: U.S. Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Committee on Governmental Affairs, The Role of the Board of Directors in Enron’s Collapse, S. Prt. 107-70, 8 July 2002
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. The report states its own evidentiary basis: "Based upon the evidence before it, including over one million pages of subpoenaed documents, interviews of 13 Enron Board members, and the Subcommittee hearing on May 7, 2002", it makes six numbered findings, reproduced here in its own words. "(1) Fiduciary Failure. The Enron Board of Directors failed to safeguard Enron shareholders and contributed to the collapse of the seventh largest public company in the United States, by allowing Enron to engage in high risk accounting, inappropriate conflict of interest transactions, extensive undisclosed off-the-books activities, and excessive executive compensation. The Board witnessed numerous indications of questionable practices by Enron management over several years, but chose to ignore them to the detriment of Enron shareholders, employees and business associates." "(2) High Risk Accounting. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to engage in high risk accounting practices." "(3) Inappropriate Conflicts of Interest. Despite clear conflicts of interest, the Enron Board of Directors approved an unprecedented arrangement allowing Enron’s Chief Financial Officer to establish and operate the LJM private equity funds which transacted business with Enron and profited at Enron’s expense. The Board exercised inadequate oversight of LJM transaction and compensation controls and failed to protect Enron shareholders from unfair dealing." "(4) Extensive Undisclosed Off-The-Books Activity. The Enron Board of Directors knowingly allowed Enron to conduct billions of dollars in off-the-books activity to make its financial condition appear better than it was and failed to ensure adequate public disclosure of material off-the-books liabilities that contributed to Enron’s collapse." "(5) Excessive Compensation. The Enron Board of Directors approved excessive compensation for company executives, failed to monitor the cumulative cash drain caused by Enron’s 2000 annual bonus and performance unit plans, and failed to monitor or halt abuse by Board Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kenneth Lay of a company-financed, multi-million dollar, personal credit line." "(6) Lack of Independence. The independence of the Enron Board of Directors was compromised by financial ties between the company and certain Board members." The phrase "knowingly allowed" is the report's own, used in findings (2) and (4). This is a congressional subcommittee report about the conduct of a board. It determines no liability, and it is not a criminal or civil adjudication of any individual director.
